attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his post. The Goertzel mention backs up his claim; it is not a quote from Goertzel.

semantics.note: Accurately captures his firm present-tense claim: LLMs fall short of his AGI definition because they are unreliable and do not generalize reliably.

contract.note: The plain reading (not human-level in reliability or generalization) is ordinary. Keeping 'reliably' means partial success on new tasks does not count against him, and the period up to the post date is reasonable.

evidence.note: The benchmark operator, dated Dec 2024, says o3 is not AGI and still fails very easy tasks.
Early ARC-AGI-2 data: o3 likely under 30% versus over 95% for humans. A large gap on new tasks within the period.
Perturbation study: accuracy fell for every model when only numbers changed. The page read is v2 (Aug 2025), but v1 was posted 2024-10-07 in the period, and v2 predates the evaluation date.

o3's 75.7% on ARC-AGI-1 shows real gains on new tasks. The contract says some success does not contradict, and the same source says o3 is not human-level overall, so this does not meet the contradiction condition.

reviews.rationale: Evidence from the period shows the best system still failing easy new tasks, a large human-AI gap on fresh tasks, and accuracy losses under small changes. o3's ARC-AGI-1 jump is real progress but falls short of robust, human-comparable generalization. The support condition is met.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his post.

semantics.note: Keeps 'frequently' and 'regularly' and all four parts of the claim. A firm observation about generative AI.

contract.note: Taking 'frequently/regularly' as a meaningful, recurring rate is ordinary. Setting aside the unmeasurable 'superficial' is reasonable. The plain reading refers to normal use while the support condition accepts hard benchmarks, a mild tension noted in the stated gaps.

evidence.note: SimpleQA: no frontier model got 90% of the questions it attempted right, so false answers at meaningful rates. The questions were picked to be hard.
Models consistently overstated their confidence, which fits weak self-checking. This is a lab report on its own and rival models.
One irrelevant clause cut accuracy by up to 65% across top models on grade-school math. v1 dates from Oct 2024; v2 was read.
SimpleQA was built against GPT-4's answers, so its error rates likely run above everyday use. This tempers 'frequently'.

reviews.rationale: Studies from the period show meaningful fabrication rates, consistent overconfidence, and large drops in reasoning and math accuracy under light changes, which meets the support condition. Caveat: the measurements use hard or altered tasks rather than everyday use, and 'superficial' is not scored.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his post.

semantics.note: The statement assumes the inability as fact and draws an inference about resourcefulness. Scoring only the factual part is appropriate.

contract.note: Reading 'inability' as unable to reliably catch their own errors unaided is ordinary in context. Excluding outside tools is a reading choice he did not supply, and the result partly turns on it and on how fine-tuned self-correction is treated.

evidence.note: Peer-reviewed survey (Dec 2024): prompted LLMs show no successful self-correction except on unusually suitable tasks.
Frontier models, including o1-preview, consistently overstated their confidence. This fits weak self-checking.

Same quote as e1. Self-correction works with outside feedback, which the contract excludes, or after large-scale fine-tuning. That weakens an absolute reading but does not show reliable unaided self-correction.
2023 study with the same finding, from before the target period.

reviews.rationale: Under the contract's plain reading, evidence from the period shows prompted LLMs failing to self-correct and being consistently overconfident, so the support condition is met. Self-correction through outside feedback or fine-tuning weakens a literal absolute 'inability' but does not meet the contradiction condition.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words. Mahabal and Fraser are cited as sources of the examples, not as the claimants.

semantics.note: Revision 2 keeps his scope (the discussed variations) and his hedged parenthetical. The 'perhaps' part is rightly left unscored.

contract.note: Defining robust as consistent success on each variation across repeated trials is a fair, ordinary reading of 'robust across all the variations'. Treating the demonstration record as cumulative is reasonable.

evidence.note: Shows sensitivity to changes in math questions, but not on the Mahabal/Fraser set discussed.
Dec 2024 independent evaluation: o1 close to solving all of a related 13-prompt set. That set is different, and near-complete success neither confirms nor rules out robustness across his set.

reviews.rationale: The packet recovers no list of the discussed variations, and the Fraser and chess transcripts could not be read. No evaluation covers the full set. Related evidence shows fragility but also near-complete o1 success on a different set. Neither condition can be checked, so the claim stays unresolved.
